sources.source: AWS — DynamoDB zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift

items.item: on activation, the integration exports the full DynamoDB table, then incrementally replicates updates every fifteen to thirty minutes using DynamoDB's own incremental exports
a zero-ETL integration requires the source DynamoDB table to have point-in-time recovery enabled

The hook's fraud-detection scenario is deliberately a case where a documented cadence, not a system failure, is the actual cause — there is no bug to find anywhere in this scenario, which is exactly why reading a vendor's own documented window as a freshness SLA has to happen before adoption, not after an incident.

Naming Aurora, DynamoDB, RDS and Fabric mirroring together as instances of one mechanism matters because a learner who only remembers one vendor's name would wrongly conclude zero-ETL is a single product rather than a pattern that recurs across both major cloud platforms.

at.step: Reveal: managed CDC into an analytics engine

items.item: DynamoDB's own documented window is stated as a range, fifteen to thirty minutes, not a single guaranteed number — a learner who collapses that range to its midpoint or its best case has already made the exact mistake the Prove It step is built to catch.

Calling zero-ETL 'managed log-based CDC' is this topic's central synthesis, built from this course's own already-taught CDC vocabulary rather than from either vendor's documentation directly — FACT-CHECK states this plainly as the course's own claim, not an AWS- or Microsoft-sourced one.

The sandbox reproduction uses a real Postgres logical replication slot, drained on a fixed cycle, as the stand-in for DynamoDB's own incremental-export mechanism — this topic is explicit throughout that the reproduction models the documented cadence and prerequisite shape, not DynamoDB's own internal implementation, which this sandbox cannot run.

at.step: Reveal: reproducing the shape on this sandbox's own Postgres

items.item: The fraud order's invisibility between pulses in examples.py is asserted as a positive requirement of the test, not caught as an incidental side effect — the mechanism is working exactly as the documented cadence says it should, which is the whole point the hook opened with.

The three named costs (schema timing, filtering limits, vendor billing) are presented as a package that comes with giving up pipeline code, not as independent complaints — a team cannot selectively keep one lever (say, filtering control) while still adopting the managed integration for the others.

at.step: Reveal: the three costs of giving up pipeline control

items.item: This topic's own closing arithmetic (a twenty-minute requirement against a fifteen-to-thirty-minute documented window) generalizes past DynamoDB specifically: any fixed window whose own worst case falls at or above a stated requirement cannot be trusted to meet that requirement on every cycle, regardless of which vendor documents the window.

This topic's own 'Leaves out' line (CDC's own mechanism in depth, the streaming-lakehouse convergence ideas marked skipped in the rest of the syllabus subsection) keeps its scope to exactly what naming zero-ETL's real mechanism and costs requires, consistent with how every other topic in this chapter states its own boundaries explicitly.

Choosing Postgres's wal_level and a logical replication slot as the prerequisite-and-cursor stand-in, rather than a simpler timestamp-column polling scheme, keeps the reproduction faithful to the actual category of mechanism (a WAL reader reading a replication stream) this course already taught, rather than substituting an easier-to-build but architecturally different approximation.
